mcqs.question: What is the main downside of a write-through cache policy?
options: It can silently lose data on eviction
It requires a dirty bit per line, adding hardware complexity
It generates memory traffic on every write, even repeated writes to the same address
It cannot be combined with any placement policy
mcqs.explanation: Write-through sends every write to memory immediately, so repeated writes to the same address each cost a memory write — the bandwidth cost the policy trades away for simplicity. Losing data on eviction and needing a dirty bit are write-back concerns, not write-through's; placement policy is independent of write policy.

mcqs.question: Why does a write-back cache need a dirty bit per line?
options: To mark which lines are allowed to be evicted at all
To track whether a line's cached value differs from memory, so eviction knows whether a write-back is needed first
To speed up the tag comparison on every access
To indicate which way within a set was used most recently
mcqs.explanation: The dirty bit exists purely to answer: does memory already have this line's current value, or not? Clean lines can be dropped for free on eviction; dirty ones must be flushed to memory first. It has no role in eviction eligibility generally, tag comparison speed, or recency tracking (that's LRU's job).

mcqs.question: Why do write-back caches typically pair with write-allocate rather than no-write-allocate?
options: Write-back requires write-allocate for correctness — the pairing is mandatory
Write-allocate ensures the line is actually in cache to accumulate the deferred, batched writes that write-back is designed to exploit
No-write-allocate is incompatible with dirty bits
mcqs.explanation: The pairing isn't a hard requirement, but a natural fit: write-back's whole benefit is deferring and batching writes in cache, which only works if a write miss brings the line into cache in the first place. Dirty bits and eviction are unaffected by the allocate decision — allocate only governs whether a write-miss fetches the line.

mcqs.question: In a write-back cache, what must happen when a dirty line is chosen for eviction?
options: Nothing — the line can simply be overwritten since memory has a copy
The line must be written back to memory before being overwritten, since it holds the only current copy of that data
The dirty bit must be cleared without writing anything back
The eviction must be blocked until the CPU explicitly flushes the whole cache
mcqs.explanation: A dirty line means memory's copy is stale — the cache line is the only up-to-date version. Skipping the write-back on eviction silently discards that update. Clearing the dirty bit without writing back would just be a mislabeled version of the same bug, and blocking the whole cache isn't necessary — only that one line needs flushing.
